passage:
I'm Urmila, and I was ten when my friend Ankita's mother died. The next Monday, Ankita came to school and sat at her desk without speaking. Everyone was whispering, "What do we say?"
I did not know either. At lunch I took my skipping rope and sat down next to Ankita on the bench. I did not say anything, I just held out one handle. Ankita looked at it for a long time. Then she took it. We skipped slowly, and after a while Ankita said, "She used to count for me."
I said, "Show me how she counted." We counted together till the bell rang.

qa.q: What did Urmila hold out to Ankita at lunch?
qa.a: Urmila held out one handle of the skipping rope.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when everyone whispered "What do we say?"
qa.a: Urmila felt unsure and did not know what to say either. Choosing to sit and hold out a handle shows the wish to help without words.

qa.q: What did Urmila choose to do instead of trying to find the right words?
qa.a: Urmila sat next to Ankita and offered a handle of the skipping rope, then asked Ankita to show how the mother counted. Being there and doing something ordinary helped.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ankita when Urmila held out the handle?
qa.a: Ankita might have felt a little less alone, since nobody had asked anything and there was something simple to do. Saying "She used to count for me" shows the door opened.

grounding: A child whose friend lost a mother sits beside them and offers a skipping rope, and ordinary activity brings comfort.

passage:
Teacher's note, Wednesday. Pankaj came back to class after his mother's death and sat alone at the window. Most children kept a nervous distance. Rekha, nine, walked over at play-time with her wooden puzzle box and sat on the floor next to him. She did not speak. After a bit she pushed the box towards him and said, "I can't do the last piece. Can you?"
Pankaj looked at it, then turned the piece round and fitted it in. They did another. By the end of the break Pankaj had said three sentences.
I told Rekha, quietly, that what she did was kind.
Neelam, class teacher

qa.q: What did Rekha bring over to sit next to Pankaj?
qa.a: Rekha brought her wooden puzzle box.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling as she walked over and sat beside Pankaj without speaking?
qa.a: Rekha seems caring and a little shy, choosing to sit near without pressure. The puzzle was a gentle way to offer company.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that helped Pankaj join in?
qa.a: Rekha sat beside Pankaj, said she could not do the last piece and asked for help. Doing something ordinary together opened a small conversation.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt when Rekha pushed the puzzle box towards him?
qa.a: Pankaj probably felt relieved to be included without questions about his mother. Fitting the piece in and speaking three sentences show he felt safe enough.

grounding: A child sits beside a boy who lost his mother and offers a puzzle, and the ordinary activity comforts.

passage:
"Suraj, can I sit here?"
"...Okay."
"Ma said your papa died. I'm really sorry."
"..."
"I brought my new top. The red one. Want to spin it?"
"I don't feel like it."
"Okay. I'll just sit, then."
"..."
"Shankar?"
"Hmm?"
"Does it spin long?"
"Really long. Try it."
"...Ha. It's still going."
"Told you."
"Can you come tomorrow also?"
"I'll come every day. At lunch. On this step."
"Okay."

qa.q: What did Shankar bring to Suraj?
qa.a: Shankar brought the new top, the red one.

qa.q: How might Suraj have been feeling when saying no to the top?
qa.a: Suraj was probably very sad and numb after Papa's death, with no energy for play.

qa.q: Which of Shankar's choices helped Suraj?
qa.a: Shankar said sorry, offered the top, and when Suraj said no, just sat there quietly, letting Suraj join in when ready.

qa.q: What was it like for Suraj to have Shankar there?
qa.a: Suraj likely felt comforted and less alone, which is why Suraj asked Shankar to come again tomorrow.

grounding: A child whose friend lost a parent sits beside the friend and offers a toy, and presence comforts more than words.

passage:
My name is Elizabeth, and when I was in Class 4, my friend Hrithik's mother died. When he came back to school, nobody knew what to say, so nobody said anything. He sat alone at lunch.
I didn't know what to say either. So I sat next to him and opened my tiffin. I had idli. I pushed one towards him. He took it.
The next day I brought my comic book and we read it together, not talking. The day after, we played hopscotch.
Once he said, "At home everyone cries." I said, "You can play here."
I don't think I said anything clever. But he told me, years later, that the hopscotch was the first time he laughed after.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth bring the next day?
qa.a: Elizabeth brought a comic book, and they read it together.

qa.q: What was Hrithik likely feeling when he sat alone at lunch?
qa.a: Hrithik was probably sad and lonely, as nobody knew what to say to him.

qa.q: What worked better than finding the right words?
qa.a: Sitting beside him, sharing food and doing ordinary things like reading and hopscotch gave Hrithik company without pressure.

qa.q: What did school mean to Hrithik in those weeks?
qa.a: For Hrithik, school became a break from the crying at home, a place where he could play and laugh again.

grounding: A child whose friend lost a parent sits beside him and shares food and games, and presence comforts more than words.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Monday
Noor came back to school today, two weeks after her mother's death. She was quiet at assembly and sat very still in class. At break she stayed at her desk.
Reena, who sits two rows away, went over without being asked. She did not say much. She put her box of coloured pencils on Noor's desk and said, "Want to colour the mandala with me?" Noor nodded. They coloured together for the whole break. I saw Noor smile once, when Reena coloured outside the lines.
After break Reena asked me if she could sit next to Noor for the week. I agreed.
What I did next: I called Noor's father to tell him she had a friend beside her, and I will check in with Noor privately each morning this week.

qa.q: What did Reena put on Noor's desk?
qa.a: She put her box of coloured pencils on Noor's desk.

qa.q: What does Noor staying at her desk at break suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Noor was feeling sad and withdrawn, not ready to join others after her mother's death.

qa.q: What did Reena do that helped?
qa.a: Reena sat with Noor and offered to colour together without many words, giving comfort through an ordinary activity.

qa.q: How might Noor's father feel after the teacher's call?
qa.a: He might feel relieved and grateful to know Noor had a caring friend beside her at school.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child sitting with a friend who lost a parent and offering to colour together, comforting through presence.

Friday. Yusuf's diary.
Nazia came back to school today. Her abbu died last week. Everyone went quiet when she walked in, and Riya said "sorry for your loss" like a grown-up, and Nazia just looked at the floor. I didn't know what to say. So at lunch I sat next to her on the steps and didn't say anything. Then I took out my new bouncy ball and bounced it to her. She caught it. She bounced it back. We did that till the bell. She didn't smile exactly, but she said, "Can you bring it Monday?" I told Ammi, and Ammi said sometimes sitting beside someone is the kindest thing. I'm bringing the ball Monday.

qa.q: What did Yusuf bounce to Nazia?
qa.a: Yusuf's new bouncy ball.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf sit next to Nazia without saying anything?
qa.a: Yusuf felt unsure what to say and a bit nervous, but did not want Nazia to be alone.

qa.q: What could Yusuf keep doing in the weeks ahead?
qa.a: Keep sitting with Nazia and bringing ordinary games like the ball, and let her talk about her abbu only if she wants to.

qa.q: What might the bouncing game have been like for Nazia?
qa.a: It gave Nazia something ordinary and quiet to do with someone beside her, without having to talk, which seemed to comfort her enough to ask for it again.

grounding: Shows a child whose classmate's father has died sitting beside her and sharing a ball game, which comforts more than words.
